steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) are both long chains of nucleotides, but they differ in several fundamental ways:

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose, lacking an oxygen atom at the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA contains ribose, which has that 2′-OH group. The extra oxygen makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses A, G, C, but replaces thymine with uracil (U).

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold back on itself to create diverse 3-D shapes (hairpins, loops, etc.).

4. Function  
   • DNA is the long-term hereditary blueprint, storing nearly all genetic information.  
   • RNA plays many roles: messenger RNA (mRNA) conveys DNA instructions to ribosomes; transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids for protein synthesis; ribosomal RNA (rRNA) forms core parts of ribosomes; and numerous small RNAs regulate gene expression and splicing.

5. Cellular location  
   • DNA remains mainly in the nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions largely in the cytoplasm; some specialized RNAs stay in the nucleus.

6. Stability and longevity  
   • DNA’s double helix and absence of the 2′-OH make it highly stable—ideal for long-term storage.  
   • RNA’s 2′-OH and single-stranded nature render it prone to enzymatic degradation, suiting its often transient roles.

7. Replication versus transcription  
   • DNA is replicated by DNA polymerases before cell division, producing exact copies.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA by RNA polymerase; it is not typically replicated (except in certain viruses).

In short, DNA is the durable archive of genetic information, while RNA is the versatile, short-lived interpreter and executor of that information.
